answer.rationale: Audit note first: every item is a consolidated summary with the source archived, so none carries effect sizes, sample sizes, observation windows, segment definitions, or counterfactuals. I am treating them as directionally reliable priors, not as measured evidence for the revenue objective. I ranked them by distance between what each claims and what the objective requires (durable, qualified, revenue). memory_57 rates highest (4) because it is the only one that names qualified revenue AND checks a durability guard (no retention harm); it still lacks magnitude and applies only to established customers. memory_44 (3) reports pipeline quality, which is a genuine quality filter but sits upstream of closed and retained revenue, and it omits cost-to-serve for sales-assisted flows. memory_31 (3) claims a 'durable' lift, which is the right adjective, but the outcome is first-week activation with no chain to revenue. memory_86 (2) offers completion and time-to-value proxies with no revenue or retention linkage. memory_73 (2) is the most seductive right now given the competitor's entry pricing, and precisely for that reason it deserves scrutiny: it asserts acquisition and revenue lift while omitting margin, discount cohort retention, and whether the revenue persisted past the promo window; discount-acquired accounts are the classic case where short-run revenue and sustainable qualified revenue diverge. memory_91 is weakest (1): week-one engagement and 'first meaningful action' are the shallowest proxies in the set, over the shortest horizon, with no durability claim and no revenue linkage at all. Important caveat for the decision that follows: memory_91 and memory_86 are the most topically relevant to the activation and onboarding declines, but topical relevance is not evidential strength, and the two current declines are symptoms whose cause is undiagnosed. The strength of a prior should not be inferred from how conveniently it matches this week's dashboard.
